facts.text: It is Bhutan’s principal school for teaching the country’s traditional arts and crafts.
The institute teaches the thirteen traditional arts and crafts known in Bhutanese as Zorig Chusum.
Its curriculum includes disciplines such as painting, woodcarving, sculpture, embroidery, weaving and metalwork.
The school was established in 1971 to preserve and transmit Bhutan’s traditional artistic skills.
It is located in Thimphu, Bhutan’s capital, in the western part of the country.
Kuang Si Waterfall is a multi-tiered waterfall system on the Kuang Si River.
The main cascade falls over limestone terraces from a height of about 50 metres.
The waterfall forms a series of naturally calcified, blue-green pools below the main drop.
It lies in a forested limestone landscape in Luang Prabang Province, southwest of Luang Prabang.
The COPE Visitor Centre is an educational centre about the effects of unexploded ordnance in Laos and the rehabilitation of people affected by it.
It is operated by the Cooperative Orthotic and Prosthetic Enterprise, commonly known as COPE.
The centre’s exhibitions cover prosthetic and orthotic devices, rehabilitation, and the continuing human impact of wartime bombing in Laos.
Its subject is closely connected with unexploded ordnance left from the Second Indochina War, particularly the bombing of Laos between 1964 and 1973.
The centre is located in Vientiane, Laos’s capital, in Vientiane Prefecture.
The Plain of Jars is an archaeological landscape containing thousands of large stone jars and associated stone features.
The jars are generally dated to the Iron Age, roughly between 500 BCE and 500 CE.
The jar sites are distributed across the Xiangkhouang Plateau in northeastern Laos.
Most jars are carved from sandstone, with some made from other local rocks including granite, limestone and breccia.
The sites are associated with prehistoric funerary practices, although their exact cultural interpretation remains under study.
The Megalithic Jar Sites in Xiengkhuang were inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2019.
Ban Nam Yang is a Tai Lue village in northern Laos, in Luang Namtha Province.
The village is known for traditional handwoven cotton textiles made on manually operated looms.
Household weaving produces cotton scarves, tablecloths and decorative wall hangings.
